questions.title: What is the legal standard for a court to retain jurisdiction over a claim for statutory penalties when the alleged wrongful conduct may have ceased?
questions.question_body: In the opinion, the court vacated summary judgment on Cohen’s MFLSA penalty claim, saying it may be moot if Consilio’s overtime policy was no longer in place. How does the court determine whether a civil penalty claim is still actionable when the defendant has allegedly stopped the conduct that violated the statute? What authorities guide the decision to retain or dismiss jurisdiction in such cases?

questions.title: Does a Minnesota employee have standing to recover civil penalties under the MPWA when the penalties must be paid to the Commissioner, not the employee?
questions.question_body: The court concluded that only the Commissioner can enforce the daily‑average‑wage penalty under § 181.101(a) of the MPWA, and the employee cannot collect the penalty. How does this affect the employee’s standing? Is the employee allowed to sue for those penalties at all, or is standing limited to the wage and liquidated‑damage components? What precedent supports limiting an employee’s claim to the wage portion only?

questions.title: How should a court interpret the phrase “provide notice” in the MWTA when an employee claims the employer failed to notify of an overtime policy change?
questions.question_body: The opinion dismissed Cohen’s MWTA claim, citing the absence of statutory authority for civil penalties under that statute. What is the statutory meaning of “provide notice” under Minn. Stat. Ann. § 181.032(f) and (d)(4)? Can a failure to notify an employee of a policy change be actionable, and if so, is it actionable through penalties or merely a wage‑payment claim?

questions.title: What is the proper procedure for a party that wants to seek injunctive relief but has not yet filed the appropriate amended complaint?
questions.question_body: Cohen attempted to obtain an injunction in his summary‑judgment brief after the trial court had already dismissed the claim. The court said the issue was not properly before it. Under what circumstances can a judge consider a new claim for injunctive relief that was not raised in the original complaint or in filing a proper amended complaint?

questions.title: Is a statutory penalty reversible or subject to summary judgment if the employee has already been paid the wages and liquidated damages they are owed?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed that the employee was paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages, yet it vacated the summary judgment on the penalty claim. If the employee has already been compensated, can the court still allow a penalty claim to proceed? How does the distinction between wage‑payment relief and penalty relief affect the viability of the claim?

questions.title: How does the court apply the plain‑meaning, unambiguous rule to determine whether the MPWA allows employees to recover penalties?
questions.question_body: The opinion relied on the *Allan v. R.D. Offutt* principle that when a statute’s language is plain, it is presumed to reflect legislative intent. The court examined § 181.101(a) and concluded that only the Commissioner can charge penalties. What specific language in § 181.101 led the court to that conclusion, and could the employee have argued that the statute’s language was ambiguous or that the Legislature intended to give employees the right to seek penalties?

questions.title: Why did the court hold that the parties’ stipulation that Cohen had been paid did not preclude a penalty claim under the MFLSA?
questions.question_body: Even after a stipulation that Cohen was paid all wages and liquidated damages, the court left open the possibility of a penalty claim. Under what reasoning can a penalty claim survive a stipulation that all compensatory damages have been paid? Does the MFLSA penal clause operate independently of the compensation clause?
